title: CUET English Test 1
subject: English (Code: 101)
syllabus_source: CUET SYLLABUS/English - 101.pdf (NTA syllabus for CUET (UG) 2026, latest published)

instructions: Each correct answer earns 5 marks; each incorrect answer deducts 1 mark; unattempted questions earn 0.
The last 15 questions are three passage sets (factual, narrative, literary) of 5 questions each; each set stays together.

questions.question:
Choose the word most opposite in meaning to the word in capitals:
The manager's reply was so AMBIGUOUS that nobody knew whether the plan had been approved.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Explicit
Why: Ambiguous means open to more than one meaning; explicit means stated clearly and plainly.
Why not the others: (A) and (C) are near-synonyms. (B) is unrelated.
Key point: The sentence shows the meaning: nobody could tell what was meant.

questions.question:
Match the words in List-I with their definitions in List-II:

List-I
(A) Insomnia
(B) Omnipotent
(C) Pedestrian
(D) Anonymous

List-II
(I) A person who travels on foot
(II) Inability to sleep
(III) Of unknown name or authorship
(IV) Having unlimited power
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A)-(II), (B)-(IV), (C)-(I), (D)-(III)
Why: Insomnia — inability to sleep (II); omnipotent — all-powerful (IV); pedestrian — one who walks (I); anonymous — of unknown name (III).
Why not the others: (A) swaps insomnia and omnipotent; (C) swaps omnipotent and pedestrian; (D) swaps pedestrian and anonymous.
Key point: "Omni-" means all; "anonymous" comes from Greek for "without a name".

questions.question:
Select the correct pairs of antonyms:
A. timid — bold
B. lucid — obscure
C. prudent — wise
D. hostile — friendly
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: A) A, B and D only
C) B, C and D only
D) A, B, C and D
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) A, B and D only
Why: Timid (shy) and bold, lucid (clear) and obscure (unclear), hostile and friendly are opposites.
Why not the others: Pair C is a pair of synonyms — prudent means wise and careful. Options (B), (C) and (D) include pair C.
Key point: In pair questions, test each pair on its own.

questions.question: Choose the word most similar in meaning to EPHEMERAL:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Short-lived
Why: Ephemeral means lasting a very short time.
Why not the others: (B) means delicate or heavenly, and is often confused because it sounds similar. (C) is the opposite. (D) means necessary.
Key point: Fame on social media is often ephemeral.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the most appropriate word to fill in the blank:
The results of the new experiment were ________ with the earlier findings.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) consistent
Why: After "were", an adjective is needed; "consistent with" means in agreement with.
Why not the others: (A) is a noun. (B) is a verb. (D) is an adverb.
Key point: The pattern is "be consistent with something".

questions.question:
Match the figures of speech in List-I with the examples in List-II:

List-I
(A) Oxymoron
(B) Metaphor
(C) Onomatopoeia
(D) Apostrophe

List-II
(I) The bees buzzed lazily in the hive.
(II) O wind, carry my message to the hills!
(III) Time is a thief that steals our youth.
(IV) The hall fell into a deafening silence.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A)-(IV), (B)-(III), (C)-(I), (D)-(II)
Why: "Deafening silence" joins opposites — oxymoron (IV); "Time is a thief" is a direct comparison — metaphor (III); "buzzed" imitates a sound — onomatopoeia (I); speaking to the wind as if it could hear — apostrophe (II).
Why not the others: (A) swaps oxymoron and metaphor; (B) swaps onomatopoeia and apostrophe; (C) swaps metaphor and onomatopoeia.
Key point: A metaphor says one thing is another; a simile uses "like" or "as".

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Sentence Transformation and Correctness
questions.question:
Which of the following sentences are grammatically correct?
A. Neither the teacher nor the students were present.
B. Each of the boys has a bicycle.
C. One of my friends live in Delhi.
D. The news are good today.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: A) A, B and C only
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) A and B only
Why: In A, the verb agrees with the nearer subject "students" (were). In B, "each" is singular (has).
Why not the others: C should be "lives" (the subject is "one"). D should be "is" ("news" is singular). Options (A), (B) and (C) include C or D.
Key point: Find the true subject before choosing the verb.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the most appropriate word to fill in the blank:
________ it was raining heavily, the match continued.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Although
Why: The two clauses contrast (heavy rain, yet the match went on), so a contrast linker is needed.
Why not the others: (A) and (D) show a reason. (B) shows a condition.
Key point: Although = in spite of the fact that.

questions.question: Choose the word most opposite in meaning to SCARCE:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Abundant
Why: Scarce means in short supply; abundant means plentiful.
Why not the others: (A) and (B) are close in meaning to scarce. (D) Scarce goods are often expensive, but it is not the opposite.
Key point: Scarcity is the central problem of economics.

questions.question:
Rearrange the following parts to form a meaningful sentence:
A. only twice in six months,
B. The committee, which had met
C. that the villagers had proposed
D. finally approved the plan
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) B, A, D, C
Why: "The committee, which had met" (B) is completed by "only twice in six months," (A); the main verb follows (D), and "that the villagers had proposed" (C) describes "the plan".
Why not the others: (B) breaks "had met only twice". (C) begins with a lower-case verb. (D) puts the "that" clause before "the plan" it describes.
Key point: A relative clause sits right after the noun it describes.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the correct preposition to fill in the blank:
The clerk was accused ________ stealing files from the office.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) of
Why: The verb "accuse" takes "of": accused of a crime.
Why not the others: (A) is used with "blamed for". (C) is not used with "accused". (D) is used with "charged with".
Key point: Accused of, charged with, blamed for.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the most appropriate word to fill in the blank:
The new rule will not ________ the students who have already registered.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) affect
Why: "Affect" is the verb meaning to influence or change; after "will not", a verb is needed.
Why not the others: (A) "Effect" as a verb means to bring about, which does not fit. (B) is a plural noun. (C) means fondness.
Key point: Affect is usually the verb; effect is usually the noun.

questions.question:
Select the words that can replace the phrase: "a person who cannot read or write"
A. illiterate
B. illegible
C. unlettered
D. ineligible
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: D) A, B and C only
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) A and C only
Why: "Illiterate" and "unlettered" both describe a person who cannot read or write.
Why not the others: B (illegible) describes writing that cannot be read. D (ineligible) means not qualified. Options (A), (C) and (D) include one of them.
Key point: Illegible handwriting can be written by a literate person.

questions.question:
Match the words in List-I with their meanings in List-II:

List-I
(A) Candid
(B) Frugal
(C) Lethargic
(D) Meticulous

List-II
(I) Frank and honest
(II) Careful not to waste money
(III) Sluggish and lacking energy
(IV) Very careful about details
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A)-(I), (B)-(II), (C)-(III), (D)-(IV)
Why: Candid — frank (I); frugal — thrifty (II); lethargic — sluggish (III); meticulous — careful about details (IV).
Why not the others: (B) swaps candid and frugal; (C) swaps frugal and lethargic; (D) swaps lethargic and meticulous.
Key point: Meticulous and frugal are both "careful", but about different things.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the most appropriate word to fill in the blank:
The witness gave such a ________ account of the accident that the jury believed every word.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) credible
Why: "Credible" means believable, which fits an account that the jury believed.
Why not the others: (A) means too ready to believe (it describes a listener, not an account). (B) means deserving praise. (D) is a noun meaning a qualification.
Key point: Credible describes a statement or source; credulous describes a person.

questions.question:
Rearrange the following sentences to form a coherent paragraph:
A. The pulp is then pressed into thin sheets and dried.
B. In a paper mill, wood is first cut into chips and cooked with chemicals to separate its fibres.
C. These fibres are washed and beaten into a soft pulp.
D. At the end, the dried sheets are rolled and cut to size.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) B, C, A, D
Why: B introduces the process ("first"); C continues with "These fibres"; A uses "The pulp ... then"; D ends with "At the end".
Why not the others: (A) presses the pulp before it is made. (B) refers to "These fibres" before they are mentioned. (D) cuts the sheets before they are pressed and dried.
Key point: Pronouns such as "these" and words such as "then" fix the order.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the correctly spelt word to fill in the blank:
The hotel offers comfortable ________ for forty guests.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) accommodation
Why: The correct spelling has double "c" and double "m": accommodation.
Why not the others: (A) has one "m". (C) has one "c". (D) has "a" in place of the second "o".
Key point: Accommodation is large enough for two Cs and two Ms.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the correct preposition to fill in the blank:
She is very good ________ solving puzzles.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) at
Why: The fixed expression is "good at" doing something.
Why not the others: (B), (C) and (D) do not follow "good" in this sense ("good with" is used with people or tools).
Key point: Many adjectives take a fixed preposition.

questions.question:
Rearrange the following parts to form a meaningful sentence:
A. to watch the sun set
B. tourists climb the old fort on the hill
C. behind the distant lake
D. Every evening,
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) D, B, A, C
Why: The sentence opens with the time phrase "Every evening," (D), then the subject and verb "tourists climb the old fort on the hill" (B), the purpose "to watch the sun set" (A), and where the sun sets, "behind the distant lake" (C).
Why not the others: (A) puts the capitalised opener in the middle. (C) gives the purpose before the subject. (D) splits the purpose from where the sun sets.
Key point: A capital letter and a comma often mark the opening part.

questions.question:
Rearrange the following parts to form a meaningful sentence:
A. hundreds of commuters still use it daily
B. because there is no other route
C. Although the bridge was declared
D. unsafe last year,
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) C, D, A, B
Why: "Although the bridge was declared" (C) needs its complement "unsafe last year," (D); the main clause follows (A), and the reason comes last (B).
Why not the others: (A) separates "declared" from "unsafe". (B) and (D) start with a lower-case part.
Key point: "Although" opens a clause that is completed before the main clause.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the most appropriate phrasal verb to fill in the blank:
Riya really ________ her grandmother; both of them love music and laugh in the same way.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) takes after
Why: "Take after" means to resemble an older relative in looks or character.
Why not the others: (B) means to take control. (C) means to start a hobby or job. (D) means to absorb or to deceive.
Key point: "Take after" is used for resembling an older family member.

questions.question:
Match the phrasal verbs in List-I with their meanings in List-II:

List-I
(A) Put off
(B) Put up with
(C) Put across
(D) Put down (a revolt)

List-II
(I) Postpone
(II) Tolerate
(III) Communicate an idea clearly
(IV) Suppress by force
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A)-(I), (B)-(II), (C)-(III), (D)-(IV)
Why: Put off a meeting — postpone it (I); put up with noise — tolerate it (II); put across an idea — communicate it clearly (III); put down a revolt — suppress it (IV).
Why not the others: (B) swaps put off and put up with; (C) swaps put up with and put across; (D) swaps put across and put down.
Key point: The particle (off, up with, across, down) changes the meaning of "put".

questions.question: Choose the one word for: "A person who is new to a job or activity"
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Novice
Why: A novice is a beginner.
Why not the others: (A) is the opposite — a person with long experience. (B) as an adjective means new, but it describes ideas, not people. (C) is an official who certifies documents.
Key point: "Nov-" means new, but only novice names a person.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Sentence Transformation and Correctness
questions.sub_topic: Reported speech with will and tomorrow
questions.question:
Choose the option that best expresses the sentence in indirect speech:
She said to me, "I will finish the project tomorrow."
options: A) She told me that she would finish the project the next day.
B) She told me that I will finish the project tomorrow.
C) She said to me that she will finish the project the next day.
D) She told me that she would finish the project tomorrow.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) She told me that she would finish the project the next day.
Why: With a past reporting verb, "will" becomes "would", "I" becomes "she", and "tomorrow" becomes "the next day"; "said to me" becomes "told me".
Why not the others: (B) changes the pronoun wrongly and keeps "will". (C) keeps "will". (D) keeps "tomorrow".
Key point: Change tense, pronouns and time words together.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the most appropriate word to fill in the blank:
Heavy rain is likely tonight, so please ________ precautions before you travel.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) take
Why: The fixed collocation is "take precautions".
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (C) do not go with "precautions".
Key point: Take care, take precautions, take steps.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the most appropriate word to fill in the blank:
You will not be allowed into the examination hall ________ you show your admit card.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) unless
Why: "Unless" means "if not": you will not be allowed in if you do not show the card.
Why not the others: (A) and (C) show contrast. (D) gives a reason, which makes no sense here.
Key point: Do not use "not" again after "unless".

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the most appropriate word to fill in the blank:
Everyone ________ Ravi had finished the test when the bell rang.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) except
Why: "Except" means "but not" or "leaving out"; everyone but Ravi had finished.
Why not the others: (A) means to receive or agree to. (C) means to think something will happen. (D) is a short extract from a text.
Key point: Accept and except sound alike but differ in meaning.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the most appropriate word to fill in the blank:
After weeks of ________ rain, the river burst its banks.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) incessant
Why: "Incessant" means continuing without stopping; weeks of non-stop rain explains the flood.
Why not the others: (B), (C) and (D) all suggest little rain, which would not make the river burst its banks.
Key point: Context ("burst its banks") decides the word.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the most appropriate word to fill in the blank:
Her ________ to detail made her the best editor in the team.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) attention
Why: After the possessive "Her" and before "to detail", a noun is needed: "attention to detail".
Why not the others: (B) is an adjective. (C) is a verb. (D) is an adverb.
Key point: Check what part of speech the blank needs.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Sentence Transformation and Correctness
questions.question:
Choose the option that best expresses the sentence in the passive voice:
The workers are repairing the road near the school.
options: A) The road near the school was being repaired by the workers.
B) The road near the school has been repaired by the workers.
C) The road near the school is being repaired by the workers.
D) The road near the school is repaired by the workers.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) The road near the school is being repaired by the workers.
Why: The present continuous "are repairing" becomes "is being repaired" in the passive, with the object "the road" as the new subject.
Why not the others: (A) changes the tense to the past. (B) changes it to the present perfect. (D) changes it to the simple present.
Key point: Keep the tense when changing the voice.

questions.question:
Choose the word most similar in meaning to the word in capitals:
The climbers began the ARDUOUS ascent to the summit before dawn.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Strenuous
Why: Arduous means needing great effort; a strenuous climb needs great effort.
Why not the others: (A) and (B) are close to opposites. (C) means careless of danger.
Key point: Read the sentence: an ascent to a summit before dawn suggests effort.

questions.question: Choose the word most similar in meaning to BENEVOLENT:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Kind
Why: Benevolent means well-meaning and kindly.
Why not the others: (A) Benevolent people may or may not be rich. (C) is its opposite. (D) is unrelated.
Key point: "Bene-" means well, as in benefit.

questions.question:
Match the idioms in List-I with their meanings in List-II:

List-I
(A) A blessing in disguise
(B) To cut corners
(C) To hit the nail on the head
(D) To burn the midnight oil

List-II
(I) To work or study late into the night
(II) Something that seems bad at first but turns out to be good
(III) To say exactly the right thing about a situation
(IV) To do something cheaply or carelessly to save time or money
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A)-(II), (B)-(IV), (C)-(III), (D)-(I)
Why: A blessing in disguise — good that first looked bad (II); cut corners — skimp to save time or money (IV); hit the nail on the head — say exactly what is right (III); burn the midnight oil — work late at night (I).
Why not the others: (A) swaps cut corners and hit the nail on the head; (B) swaps the first two; (D) swaps the last two.
Key point: Learn idioms as whole units of meaning.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the correctly used word to fill in the blank:
Please buy some ________ for the office — pens, paper and envelopes.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) stationery
Why: "Stationery" (with -ery) means writing materials such as pens and paper.
Why not the others: (A) "Stationary" (with -ary) means not moving. (B) and (D) are forms of "station".
Key point: Stationery has "e" for envelopes.

questions.question:
Rearrange the following parts to complete the sentence that begins: "Doctors now advise that,"
A. rather than long workouts once a week,
B. is better for the heart
C. moderate exercise every day,
D. for most adults,
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) D, C, A, B
Why: "Doctors now advise that, for most adults (D), moderate exercise every day (C), rather than long workouts once a week (A), is better for the heart (B)." The subject (C) must come before its verb (B), and the contrast (A) follows what it is compared with.
Why not the others: (A) begins with the contrast before its subject. (B) starts with a verb. (C) puts the verb before its subject.
Key point: Find the subject and verb first; then place the other phrases around them.

questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

Every summer, India waits for the monsoon. In April and May, the sun beats down on the subcontinent, and the land heats up far faster than the surrounding seas. Warm air over north-western India rises, creating an area of low pressure, while the air over the cooler Indian Ocean stays relatively heavy. Since winds blow from areas of high pressure to areas of low pressure, moist air from the ocean is drawn towards the land. These are the south-west monsoon winds.

The monsoon usually reaches the coast of Kerala around the first of June and covers most of the country by early July. It travels in two branches, one from the Arabian Sea and the other from the Bay of Bengal. When the Arabian Sea branch meets the Western Ghats, the air is forced to rise; it cools, and its moisture falls as heavy rain on the windward slopes. By the time the winds cross the mountains, they have lost much of their moisture, so the plateau on the other side receives far less rain. Geographers call such a dry region a rain-shadow area.

Between June and September, India receives roughly three-quarters of its annual rainfall. Kharif crops such as rice depend on it, reservoirs that supply drinking water and electricity are refilled, and wells are recharged. A delayed or weak monsoon can therefore push up food prices and slow the economy, while an unusually strong one can bring floods.

Because so much depends on these few months, the India Meteorological Department issues its first forecast in April and updates it as the season approaches. Farmers, planners and ordinary citizens follow these forecasts closely.

Question: According to the passage, around when does the monsoon usually reach the coast of Kerala?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) The first of June
Why: The passage says the monsoon "usually reaches the coast of Kerala around the first of June".
Why not the others: (A) is when the land is heating up. (B) is when it covers most of the country. (D) is the end of the rainy season.
Key point: Detail questions are answered from the exact line, not from general knowledge.

questions.sub_topic: Why the plateau gets less rain
questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

Question: Why does the plateau on the far side of the Western Ghats receive far less rain?
options: A) The winds have shed most of their moisture on the way
B) The Bay of Bengal branch of the monsoon never reaches it
C) The plateau lies far lower than the coastal plains do
D) The air above the plateau is cooler than ocean air
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) The winds have shed most of their moisture on the way
Why: The passage says that by the time the winds cross the mountains "they have lost much of their moisture", so the other side is a rain-shadow area.
Why not the others: (B) and (C) are not stated in the passage. (D) confuses this with the cause of the monsoon winds.
Key point: Rain falls on the windward side; the leeward side is the rain-shadow.

questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

Question: As used in the passage, the "windward slopes" of the Western Ghats are the slopes that:
options: A) Are sheltered from the wind
B) Are covered with thick forest
C) Lie in the rain-shadow area
D) Face the wind coming from the sea
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Face the wind coming from the sea
Why: Windward means facing the direction from which the wind blows. The moist Arabian Sea winds rise and shed rain on the side that faces them.
Why not the others: (A) and (C) describe the leeward side. (B) is not the meaning of the word.
Key point: The opposite of windward is leeward.

questions.sub_topic: What draws the monsoon winds to India
questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

Kharif crops such as rice depend on it, reservoirs that supply drinking water and electricity are refilled, and wells are recharged. A delayed or weak monsoon can therefore push up food prices and slow the economy, while an unusually strong one can bring floods.

Because so much depends on these few months, the India Meteorological Department issues its first forecast in April and updates it as the season approaches. Farmers, planners and ordinary citizens follow these forecasts closely.

Question: Which statement correctly explains, according to the passage, why moist winds blow towards India in summer?
options: A) The sea heats faster than the land, so moist air rises over the ocean and drifts north
B) The land heats faster than the sea, creating low pressure over the land that draws in ocean air
C) High pressure over north-western India pushes cool air out towards the ocean
D) The Western Ghats force dry winds to rise and pull moist air behind them
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) The land heats faster than the sea, creating low pressure over the land that draws in ocean air
Why: The passage says the land heats up faster than the sea; rising warm air makes low pressure over north-western India, and since winds blow from high to low pressure, moist ocean air is drawn in.
Why not the others: (A) reverses the heating. (C) reverses the pressure. (D) describes how rain falls on the Ghats, not why the winds come.
Key point: Watch for options that keep the right words but reverse the cause.

questions.sub_topic: Best title for the monsoon passage
questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

Every summer, India waits for the monsoon. In April and May, the sun beats down on the subcontinent, and the land heats up far faster than the surrounding seas. Warm air over north-western India rises, creating an area of low pressure, while the air over the cooler Indian Ocean stays relatively heavy. Since winds blow from areas of high pressure to areas of low pressure, moist air from the ocean is drawn towards the land. These are the south-west monsoon winds.

The monsoon usually reaches the coast of Kerala around the first of June and covers most of the country by early July. It travels in two branches, one from the Arabian Sea and the other from the Bay of Bengal. When the Arabian Sea branch meets the Western Ghats, the air is forced to rise; it cools, and its moisture falls as heavy rain on the windward slopes. By the time the winds cross the mountains, they have lost much of their moisture, so the plateau on the other side receives far less rain. Geographers call such a dry region a rain-shadow area.

Between June and September, India receives roughly three-quarters of its annual rainfall. Kharif crops such as rice depend on it, reservoirs that supply drinking water and electricity are refilled, and wells are recharged. A delayed or weak monsoon can therefore push up food prices and slow the economy, while an unusually strong one can bring floods.

Because so much depends on these few months, the India Meteorological Department issues its first forecast in April and updates it as the season approaches. Farmers, planners and ordinary citizens follow these forecasts closely.

Question: Which of the following is the most suitable title for the passage?
options: B) The History of Weather Forecasting
C) The Monsoon: How It Comes and Why It Matters
D) Crops of the Rabi Season
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) The Monsoon: How It Comes and Why It Matters
Why: The passage explains how the monsoon forms and moves, and why it matters for crops, water and the economy. The title covers both parts.
Why not the others: (A) is one small point. (B) is mentioned only at the end. (D) The passage mentions kharif, not rabi, crops.
Key point: A good title covers the whole passage, not one detail.

questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

When old Ramdas-ji retired, nobody in Sonapur wanted to look after the village library. It was only one dusty room in the panchayat building, with three shelves of books and a register that no one had signed for months. Meera, who had just finished Class 12 and was waiting for her college to open, offered to keep it open in the afternoons.

On the first day, she swept the floor, wiped every shelf and sat at the table with a book open in front of her. Nobody came. On the second day, two boys peeped in through the window, giggled and ran away. That evening Meera carried a box of picture books to the neem tree outside and began to read a story aloud, doing the voices of the tiger and the clever jackal. Within minutes, the two boys were back with their sisters. The ice was broken.

By Wednesday, the children were coming every afternoon, and some of their mothers waited to borrow cookery and health books. On Friday, an old farmer stood at the door, turning his turban in his hands. "Do you have anything about soil?" he asked. "My wheat has not done well for two years." Meera searched the shelves, found a government booklet on soil testing and copied the address of the nearest testing centre for him.

On Saturday evening, she counted the names in the register: twenty-three. It was not a large number, but as she locked the door, Meera felt that the room behind her was no longer empty.

Question: Why did Meera begin looking after the village library?
options: A) The panchayat paid her a salary for it
B) Ramdas-ji had retired, and nobody else wanted to do it
C) Her college had asked her to run it as a project
D) The children of the village had requested her to
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Ramdas-ji had retired, and nobody else wanted to do it
Why: The passage begins: "When old Ramdas-ji retired, nobody in Sonapur wanted to look after the village library." Meera, who was free until college opened, offered.
Why not the others: (A) and (C) are not mentioned. (D) The children came only after she began reading aloud.
Key point: Answer from what the passage states.

Question: In the passage, "The ice was broken" means that:
options: A) The first awkwardness had ended, and people began to come
B) The weather had suddenly become warm
C) The children had broken something in the library
D) Meera had given up trying to attract readers
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) The first awkwardness had ended, and people began to come
Why: To break the ice is to end the first stiffness or shyness in a situation. Once the children joined the story-reading, people began to use the library.
Why not the others: (B) and (C) take the idiom literally. (D) is the opposite.
Key point: Idioms in passages are read in context, not word by word.

Question: What does the old farmer's visit suggest about the library?
options: A) Only children were interested in its books
B) The farmer could not read, so Meera read to him
C) It could help adults with real problems in their work
D) It had no useful books for anyone in the village
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) It could help adults with real problems in their work
Why: The farmer came with a practical problem (his wheat had not done well), and Meera found a booklet on soil testing and the address of a testing centre. The library proved useful for adults' work, not only for stories.
Why not the others: (A) Mothers and the farmer also came. (B) This is not stated. (D) She found a useful booklet.
Key point: Inference questions ask what an event shows, not what happened.

Question: "Meera felt that the room behind her was no longer empty." This suggests that:
options: A) The room had been filled with new furniture
B) The library had become a living part of the village
C) Some children were still inside when she locked it
D) She was afraid of being alone in the building
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) The library had become a living part of the village
Why: Twenty-three names in a week showed that people now used and valued the library. "No longer empty" refers to the life it now had, not to objects or people left inside.
Why not the others: (A) and (C) read the line literally. (D) has no support.
Key point: Closing lines often carry the story's central idea.

questions.sub_topic: Figure of speech in the river's waking
questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

Before the sun had climbed over the far bank, the river was already awake. It stirred under a thin blanket of mist, stretched its grey arms along the steps of the ghat and murmured to the boats tied at its edge. The first temple bell rang out, clear and cold, and a flock of pigeons rose from the roof of the old rest-house like a handful of thrown ash.

One by one, the lamps of the evening before floated past, their flames long gone, small leaf-boats carrying nothing but the memory of light. An old woman stood waist-deep in the water, her palms joined, so still that she seemed to have grown out of the river itself. Behind her, a boatman dipped his oar — splash, drip, splash — and the silence closed again behind every stroke.

Then the light came. It did not arrive all at once; it leaked into the sky, pale as milk at first, then gold, then a fierce copper that set the water on fire. The mist dissolved as though it had been only a dream the river was having. Bells, boatmen's banter and the bargaining of flower-sellers filled the air, and the city, which had been holding its breath all night, remembered its voice.

Question: "It stirred under a thin blanket of mist, stretched its grey arms along the steps of the ghat and murmured to the boats." The main figure of speech here is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Personification
Why: The river is given human actions — stirring, stretching its arms, murmuring — so it is personified.
Why not the others: (A) There is no exaggeration. (B) No two opposite words are joined. (C) There is no "like" or "as" comparison.
Key point: Personification gives human qualities to non-human things.

Question: "The mist dissolved as though it had been only a dream the river was having." This line suggests that the mist:
options: B) Became thicker as the sun rose
D) Frightened the people at the ghat
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Disappeared gently and completely
Why: Dissolved means faded away; comparing the mist to a dream suggests it vanished softly, as a dream does on waking.
Why not the others: (A) and (B) are not described. (D) Nothing frightening happens.
Key point: Read the comparison to understand the manner of the action.

Why not the others: (B), (C) and (D) do not match the images used.

Question: What does the writer mean by saying that the city "remembered its voice"?
options: A) The people of the city began to sing hymns
B) The city became noisy and busy as the day began
C) The city recalled an old story about the river
D) A loudspeaker began to make announcements
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) The city became noisy and busy as the day began
Why: After the silent dawn, bells, boatmen's banter and bargaining "filled the air" — the city's everyday sounds returned.
Why not the others: (A), (C) and (D) are not described.
Key point: The city, like the river, is personified.
